newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - LSE computerised share system nearly complete.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - LSE computerised share system nearly complete.

text.p: The London Stock Exchange's painfully slow and expensive move to put in place an electronic system to record share ownership is nearly complete.
But brokers say a large number of private investors in Britain still want old-fashioned paper share certificates.
The big test of whether private investors are adopting to the new paperless regime will come later this year when building societies float shares on the market.
The exchange's computerised system, Crest, makes stock ownership transfers easier, cheaper and faster than its existing paper-based system.
Electronic settlement also relieves corporate registrars from the burdonsome task of physically sending share certificates to holders.
Yet Stephen Pinner, managing director at retail brokerage City Deal Services, said about 80 percent of his clientele still asks for paper certificates.
"They are used to getting their share certificates as evidence of their holdings in a company," Pinner said. "They don't understand why there has to be a change."
Thomas Anderson of Forres, Scotland is one such investor. He says he doesn't trust the new computerised system.
"When I die, my family will have difficulty tracking my holdings if there are no certificates," said the 62-year-old investor who prefers to keep the paper in a filing cabinet in his study.
Anderson, a former military man, is not new to the stock market. He said he has been buying shares since 1959.
Of course, all investors aren't like Anderson, and brokers say the complexion of the investing public is changing all the time as the number of shareholders grows.
NUMBER OF SHAREHOLDERS SET TO JUMP
There are some 10 million shareholders in Britain today, up from about three million in 1979. That number is set to jump again when building societies float shares this year.

"Those who have been used to certificates will want to keep them. But there's a new generation of investors coming to the market and they don't care about certificates -- most of them have never seen a certificate," said Justin Urquhart Stewart, director of business planning at Barclays Stock Brokers.
These newcomers, he said, have been drawn into the stock market in by the rash of privatisations and company stock schemes.
The onslaught of shares from building societies could turn an additional eight million British citizens into shareholders, Stewart said.
Stock exchanges in the United States and across of much Europe have been settling shares electronically for years. London has been slow to embrace the new technology.
David Jones, chief executive of discount brokerage Sharelink, said his firm made a strategic decision years ago to employ all available technology.
"We have actively supported and marketed electronic trading. Even before Crest came along, we weren't passing paper certificates around," said Jones.
That's why only 15 percent of Sharelink's clients ask for paper certificates, said Jones, who also is a director of Crest.
"The people who want paper certificates want them because that's what's familiar. It's the 'this is the way we've always done it, so why change' approach,'" he added.
DEVELOPMENT OF CREST
The London Stock Exchange, Europe's busiest bourse, has been struggling to rid itself of paper settlements for 17 years.
Crest was born from the ruins of Taurus, the London Stock Exchange's disasterous attempt to build a computerised settlement system in the late 1980s.
After having run up costs of 38 million pounds ($61.4 million), Taurus was abandoned in 1993, leading to the departure of the exchange's then-chief executive Peter Rowlins.

Crest was developed by a consortium of 60 financial institutions, led by the Bank of England. The first leg of its launch came in July 1996, after almost four years in development costing some 29 million pounds.
Currently, Crest is processing more than half of the FTSE 100 stocks. The transition of all FTSE 100 shares to the system is scheduled to be completed by April.
"Crest was geared up for the institutional investor rather than for private investors, but Crest has not gone down well with Joe Public," Pinner said.
Crest did not make its debut without complaints from professionals, however. Some were vehemently opposed to the pace of the transition to the electronic world.
Last autumn, they complained of slow processing times, huge backlogs of orders and software glitches. Most of those problems appear to have been smoothed out.
And retail brokers said it is only a matter of time before private investors come to accept a world without paper share certificates.

"This is a very new thing for this marketplace. Most people we deal with are not comfortable with dematerialisation," Pinner said. "We think that in 12 to 18 months, there will be a migration away from share certificates. Over the longer term, people will feel more confident in Crest once they see the benefits." ($ = 0.618 British Pounds)
